description: Selected resources for learning and practicing AI governance and agentic AI governance.

resources.title: NIST AI Risk Management Framework 1.0 and Playbook
resources.publisher: US National Institute of Standards and Technology
resources.audience: Beginners; governance, risk, security and assurance practitioners
resources.why: A practical common structure for organizing AI governance through Govern, Map, Measure and Manage. The companion Playbook makes the framework actionable.
resources.use: Map one AI use case to the four functions, select applicable Playbook actions, and assign owners and evidence requirements. Start with the [official Playbook](https://airc.nist.gov/airmf-resources/playbook/).

resources.title: NIST Generative AI Profile (AI 600-1)
resources.publisher: US National Institute of Standards and Technology
resources.audience: Governance, risk and security practitioners assessing generative AI
resources.why: Extends the AI RMF with risks and actions specific to generative AI, making a general governance program more useful for LLM systems.
resources.use: Identify generative-AI-specific risks and adapt the recommended actions into your risk treatment and evaluation plan.

resources.title: ISO/IEC 42001:2023 — AI management systems
resources.access: Paid standard; free official overview and sample
resources.audience: AI governance program owners, auditors and enterprise leaders
resources.why: Provides requirements for establishing and improving an organizational AI management system, including policies, responsibilities and management processes.
resources.use: Structure an AI management system and assess organizational gaps against the licensed standard.

resources.title: ISO/IEC 42005:2025 — AI system impact assessment
resources.access: Paid standard; free official overview and sample
resources.audience: Impact assessors, governance reviewers and responsible AI teams
resources.why: Focuses on AI's effects on individuals, groups and society, complementing organizational risk and management-system work.
resources.use: Design an impact assessment that considers affected people and revisits foreseeable impacts through the AI lifecycle.

resources.title: OECD AI Principles
resources.audience: Beginners, policy teams and global governance programs
resources.why: Supplies shared international language for trustworthy AI, human rights, transparency, robustness and accountability.
resources.use: Set the principles for an AI policy, then translate each principle into responsibilities, controls and evidence.

resources.title: OECD Due Diligence Guidance for Responsible AI
resources.audience: Enterprise governance, procurement, supplier risk and responsible AI teams
resources.why: Turns responsible-AI principles into a six-step due diligence process across the AI value chain, with implementation examples and links to related frameworks.
resources.use: Create a due diligence workflow covering adverse impacts, mitigation, monitoring, communication and remediation, including supplier relationships.

resources.title: EU AI Act — official legal text and implementation guidance
resources.audience: Governance and legal teams assessing EU-market obligations
resources.why: The authoritative starting point for determining roles, prohibited practices, high-risk classification, transparency duties and other applicable obligations.
resources.use: Determine the system's scope and your role, then verify applicable provisions and dates against the current legal text and official implementation guidance. Use the [Commission overview](https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/policies/regulatory-framework-ai) for implementation context.

resources.title: Introduction to AI assurance
resources.publisher: UK Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
resources.audience: Beginners, governance reviewers and assurance practitioners
resources.why: Explains how assurance turns claims about AI into evidence, and distinguishes impact assessment, audit, testing and other assurance techniques.
resources.use: Choose assurance methods for a specific governance claim and define what evidence reviewers should receive.

resources.title: ICO AI and data protection risk toolkit
resources.audience: Privacy, data protection and AI governance practitioners
resources.why: A practical regulator-produced tool for identifying and reducing AI risks to people's rights and freedoms.
resources.use: Use the workbook to identify data-protection risks and required actions. Check current ICO guidance before relying on it: the toolkit is under review following the Data (Use and Access) Act.

resources.title: Canada Algorithmic Impact Assessment
resources.format: Online questionnaire, guidance and completed examples
resources.access: Free; open licence for sharing and reuse
resources.audience: Impact assessors, governance teams and public-sector practitioners
resources.why: An assessment workflow for Canadian federal automated decisions, linking system context, impacts and mitigation to four impact levels, with completed assessments to learn from.
resources.use: Complete a sample assessment and compare it with published government examples. Mandatory use is limited to systems covered by Canada's Directive on Automated Decision-Making; other organizations can adapt the approach.

resources.title: UK Algorithmic Transparency Recording Standard
resources.format: Excel / Google Sheets template, guidance and published records
resources.audience: Governance, AI inventory, transparency and public-sector teams
resources.why: Provides a public summary and a detailed system record, with completed examples that show how algorithmic transparency works in practice.
resources.use: Adapt the [official template](https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/algorithmic-transparency-template) for an AI system record and compare published examples. Its mandatory requirements apply only within the stated UK public-sector scope.

resources.title: UNESCO Recommendation on the Ethics of Artificial Intelligence
resources.audience: Policy teams, educators and governance practitioners working across regions
resources.why: Keeps governance grounded in human rights, inclusion, human responsibility and environmental impacts, beyond operational and cybersecurity risk.
resources.use: Review whose rights and interests a governance assessment might overlook and incorporate those stakeholders and impacts.

resources.title: Model AI Governance Framework for Agentic AI
resources.format: Governance framework with enterprise case studies
resources.audience: GRC, cybersecurity, enterprise owners
resources.why: A practical enterprise foundation for agent permissions, human accountability, control selection, testing and monitoring, illustrated with deployment cases.
resources.use: Turn its four dimensions into an agent review checklist and identify the evidence needed before deployment.

resources.title: Practices for Governing Agentic AI Systems
resources.publisher: OpenAI; Shavit, Agarwal, Brundage et al.
resources.audience: GRC, risk owners, policy and research
resources.why: A foundational treatment of suitability, constrained actions, approvals, activity visibility, monitoring, attribution and interruptibility.
resources.use: Define who can stop an agent, which actions need approval and what records make responsibility traceable.

resources.title: Visibility into AI Agents
resources.publisher: Alan Chan et al.; ACM FAccT 2024
resources.audience: Governance reviewers, audit, research
resources.why: Connects agent identifiers, monitoring and activity records to accountability, while examining privacy and power trade-offs.
resources.use: Design an evidence and logging policy that explains which agents acted, for whom and under what oversight.

resources.title: Intelligent AI Delegation
resources.publisher: Nenad Tomašev, Matija Franklin and Simon Osindero
resources.audience: Governance designers, architects, researchers
resources.why: Proposes a framework for delegating tasks, authority and responsibility across humans and agents, with explicit boundaries and accountability.
resources.use: Review agent handoffs: delegated task, allowed scope, evidence of capability, escalation and responsibility for failure.

resources.title: The Ethics of Advanced AI Assistants
resources.publisher: Iason Gabriel et al.; Google DeepMind researchers
resources.audience: Governance, policy, product and research
resources.why: Extends agent reviews beyond cybersecurity to manipulation, user trust, privacy, autonomy, access and societal impacts.
resources.use: Select the chapters relevant to your use case when preparing impact assessments or human-agent interaction requirements.

resources.title: Demystifying Evals for AI Agents
resources.audience: Governance reviewers, evaluation teams, developers
resources.why: Explains tasks, trials, graders, traces and real outcomes, plus why repeated agent runs and human calibration matter.
resources.use: Assess whether evaluations measure successful authorized action, distinguish capability tests from regression checks, and add checks for the governance requirements of your use case.

resources.title: AI Evals: Everything You Need to Know
resources.audience: Intermediate; reviewers working with AI development teams
resources.why: Answers concrete questions about error analysis, human labels, LLM judges, guardrails and evaluating agent workflows.
resources.use: Start with 'How do I evaluate agentic workflows?' and 'What's the difference between guardrails & evaluators?'; translate the answers into evidence requests.

resources.title: Careful Adoption of Agentic AI Services
resources.publisher: ASD ACSC, CISA, NSA, Canadian Centre for Cyber Security, NCSC-NZ and NCSC-UK
resources.audience: Security, enterprise operators, government and critical infrastructure
resources.why: Lifecycle guidance for privilege, configuration, behaviour, structural and accountability risks, including prerequisites for deploying agents.
resources.use: Compare a proposed deployment with its design, development, deployment and operations recommendations; identify gaps before rollout.

resources.title: OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications 2026
resources.audience: Security, GRC, developers
resources.why: A compact security baseline specifically for autonomous agents, covering threats beyond the single prompt-response interaction.
resources.use: Seed an agent threat register and security review; turn relevant risks into concrete test cases and control evidence.

resources.title: MITRE ATLAS
resources.format: Threat knowledge base / case studies / Navigator
resources.audience: Threat modeling, cybersecurity, red teams
resources.why: Connects AI attack techniques to documented cases and mitigations, giving security reviews a shared vocabulary and evidence base.
resources.use: Map a short, relevant attack path for an agent and prioritize the controls and tests that interrupt it.

resources.title: Agentic AI Threat Modeling Framework: MAESTRO
resources.audience: Security architects, threat modelers
resources.why: A structured way to examine risks across agent architecture layers and the dependencies between them.
resources.use: Decompose an agent system before reviewing model, data, execution, monitoring, security and ecosystem threats.

resources.title: MCP Security Best Practices
resources.audience: Security, IAM, architects, developers
resources.why: Concrete controls for tool-connected agents, including consent, token audiences, confused-deputy risks and unsafe proxy behaviour.
resources.use: Review MCP authorization and trust boundaries with engineering; require evidence that server and client controls match the deployed protocol version.

resources.title: The lethal trifecta for AI agents: private data, untrusted content, and external communication
resources.audience: Beginner–intermediate; governance, security and architecture teams
resources.why: Provides a memorable way to recognize when prompt injection could turn an agent's legitimate capabilities into a data-exfiltration path.
resources.use: Map each of the three capabilities to the agent's tools and data flows; require controls wherever they intersect.

resources.title: OWASP GenAI LLM Top 10 2026
resources.audience: Security teams, application owners and governance reviewers
resources.why: A practical baseline for LLM application security, with attack scenarios and mitigations that complement agent-specific risks.
resources.use: Use the applicable risks to review an LLM application's data flows and controls, then extend the review with the Agentic Top 10 when it can take actions.

resources.title: Guidelines for Secure AI System Development
resources.publisher: UK NCSC, CISA and international partner agencies
resources.audience: Security leaders, suppliers and AI system owners
resources.why: Covers secure design, development, deployment, operation and maintenance across the AI system lifecycle.
resources.use: Add the relevant supply-chain, documentation, release and monitoring questions to a design or supplier review.

resources.title: VerifyWise
resources.access: BSL 1.1 source-available; internal self-hosting under its grant. External hosting requires a commercial license; infrastructure costs apply. Paid hosted plans.
resources.audience: GRC, risk owners and governance teams; browser-based daily use, technical administration for self-hosting
resources.why: Connects AI inventories, risks, controls, owners, evidence and approvals in a practical governance workspace.
resources.use: Register an AI use case, assign its owner, document risk treatment and attach test evidence; generate a review report. The workspace organizes evidence but does not establish compliance or control effectiveness by itself.

resources.title: AI Verify Toolkit
resources.access: Apache 2.0; no toolkit license fee; infrastructure and technical setup required
resources.audience: AI assurance teams with ML/engineering support
resources.why: Provides a structured route from responsible-AI principles to technical tests and process evidence for conventional machine learning.
resources.use: Test supported supervised classification/regression models using tabular or image data and assemble assurance evidence. Scope is not general autonomous-agent validation; use Moonshot for LLM application evaluation.

resources.title: Project Moonshot
resources.format: Open-source evaluation toolkit with web UI, CLI and APIs
resources.access: Apache 2.0; local installation is free; connected model endpoints, LLM judges and compute may incur charges
resources.audience: Compliance and assurance reviewers using a configured web UI; engineers configure endpoints and tests
resources.why: Combines structured benchmarks and red-team testing with recipes and guided workflows for IMDA's LLM application safety testing starter kit.
resources.use: Run a chosen safety-test recipe, inspect an HTML report and export raw JSON results as review evidence. Benchmark coverage and grader accuracy must be judged for the actual use case.

resources.title: Microsoft PyRIT
resources.format: Open-source red-team framework, scanner and graphical interface
resources.access: MIT; framework is free; attacker, target and scoring model APIs or compute may cost money
resources.audience: Security testers and engineers; human reviewers can use a configured CoPyRIT UI
resources.why: Supports repeatable multi-turn adversarial campaigns with configurable targets, attack strategies, scoring and persistent evidence.
resources.use: Test a scoped failure objective, inspect conversations and scores, then rerun after remediation. Automated attack success labels require human validation and do not establish complete risk coverage.

resources.title: NVIDIA garak
resources.access: Apache 2.0; scanner is free; target API calls, local model hardware and compute can cost money
resources.audience: Cybersecurity practitioners comfortable with terminal commands and endpoint configuration
resources.why: Provides a practical baseline scan across prompt injection, leakage, jailbreaks and other unwanted LLM behaviors.
resources.use: Run selected probes against an authorized test endpoint and retain attempt-level JSONL records and failure rates. Pair broad scanning with application-specific agent tests; a clean scan is not proof of safety.

resources.title: Promptfoo
resources.format: Open-source CLI/library with browser results viewer
resources.access: MIT core; free community tier; some hosted red-team generation/grading features have usage limits and paid enterprise options. Target/judge model API charges are separate.
resources.audience: Engineers and technical assurance analysts; reviewers can inspect browser reports
resources.why: Turns governance requirements into repeatable pass/fail checks that can run after prompt, model or application changes.
resources.use: Build a small test set for prohibited actions and required behavior, compare versions, and preserve results in release evidence. Review grader quality and cloud-backed data flows before using sensitive examples.

resources.title: Inspect AI
resources.publisher: UK AI Security Institute and Meridian Labs
resources.access: MIT; free framework; model APIs and sandbox infrastructure may incur charges
resources.audience: Technical AI assurance teams and researchers; governance reviewers can inspect logs
resources.why: Supports evaluating complete tool-using agent tasks with reusable datasets, scorers, sandboxing and detailed transcripts.
resources.use: Define an agent task and acceptance criteria, run it in a sandbox, and review the transcript with scores. Criteria and recorded context must cover delegated authority and approval requirements; the framework does not supply those governance judgments automatically.

resources.title: Arize Phoenix
resources.access: Elastic License 2.0 source-available; self-hosting permitted subject to license restrictions. Infrastructure and evaluator APIs may cost money; managed commercial products are separate.
resources.audience: Engineers instrument applications; risk reviewers inspect traces and annotate evidence in the UI
resources.why: Makes agent tool calls, retrieval, model calls and evaluation results inspectable so reviewers can investigate what happened.
resources.use: Trace an agent run, inspect tool activity, annotate failures and compare a corrected version on the same dataset. Explicitly record authority, policy versions and approvals; ordinary traces alone may not capture that context.

resources.title: AgentDojo
resources.publisher: ETH Zurich and Invariant Labs researchers
resources.format: Open-source benchmark environment with paper and trace examples
resources.access: MIT; free benchmark code and published results; rerunning model-based tests may incur API/compute costs
resources.audience: Technical security and assurance practitioners; non-coders can study published traces
resources.why: Tests whether tool-using agents complete legitimate tasks while resisting prompt injection, making the utility/security tradeoff observable.
resources.use: Run or inspect a task under an attack and a defense; compare legitimate task success, attack success and the full action trace. Transfer findings cautiously: benchmark scenarios are not an enterprise's real controls or deployment environment.

resources.title: Fairlearn
resources.format: Open-source Python library, examples and practitioner guide
resources.access: MIT; free library and learning materials; local data/compute required
resources.audience: Data scientists and quantitative auditors; GRC practitioners can use the assessment guide with technical support
resources.why: Provides methods for assessing differences in model performance and outcomes across groups, with guidance on mitigation and trade-offs.
resources.use: Compare error rates or outcomes across relevant groups, examine uncertainty and document mitigation tradeoffs. Fairness is context-dependent; a metric does not establish legal compliance, justice or due process.

resources.title: MIT AI Risk Repository
resources.publisher: MIT AI Risk Initiative / MIT FutureTech and collaborators
resources.audience: Risk assessors, researchers, evaluators and educators
resources.why: Provides a searchable inventory of AI risks tied to source literature, with causal and domain classifications that expose gaps in narrow risk registers.
resources.use: Filter risks relevant to your use case, inspect the source evidence, and convert applicable risks into contextual risk statements. Assess likelihood and severity for your own context; the repository does not supply those scores.

resources.title: AI Incident Database
resources.audience: Governance, risk, assurance and incident-response teams; educators
resources.why: Makes governance concrete through reported real-world failures, with linked reports that can inform risk workshops and incident exercises.
resources.use: Select a relevant case, inspect its original reporting, and distinguish reported facts from allegations before identifying possible control and ownership failures.

resources.title: Closing the AI Accountability Gap
resources.publisher: Inioluwa Deborah Raji et al. / ACM FAT* 2020
resources.format: Research paper and linked audit templates
resources.audience: Governance leads, internal auditors and assurance reviewers
resources.why: Connects lifecycle decisions to a documented internal audit process, including the evidence an audit must leave behind.
resources.use: Use the paper's audit framework to plan one internal AI audit and identify the documents needed at each stage before testing begins.

resources.title: Model Cards for Model Reporting
resources.publisher: Margaret Mitchell et al. / ACM FAT* 2019
resources.audience: Model reviewers, procurement teams and technical owners
resources.why: Establishes a practical model documentation format covering intended use, evaluation conditions and performance across relevant groups.
resources.use: Ask a supplier for intended uses, exclusions, evaluation methods and disaggregated results; record which facts still need independent evidence. Use the current [Hugging Face model-card guide](https://huggingface.co/docs/hub/model-cards) for implementation.

resources.title: Datasheets for Datasets
resources.publisher: Timnit Gebru et al. / Communications of the ACM
resources.audience: Data owners, privacy teams and governance reviewers
resources.why: Makes data provenance, collection choices, intended uses and limitations visible before a dataset is reused.
resources.use: Apply its questions to one training or evaluation dataset, then adapt them to a retrieval corpus and identify missing provenance. See the practical [dataset-card guide](https://huggingface.co/docs/hub/datasets-cards).

resources.title: Ethics of AI
resources.format: Self-paced course with readings and exercises
resources.access: Free; sign-in for progress, assignments and completion certificate
resources.audience: Beginner; governance, policy and business professionals
resources.why: A rigorous, accessible foundation in accountability, transparency, human rights and fairness, with exercises rather than a glossary alone.
resources.use: Start with Accountability and AI Ethics in Practice; use the exercises to identify affected people and challenge an AI deployment rationale.

resources.title: IAPP Artificial Intelligence Governance Professional (AIGP) Training
resources.access: Paid; MyIAPP account required; exam is a separate purchase
resources.audience: Beginner–intermediate; professionals establishing a governance knowledge baseline
resources.why: Structured coverage of the AI lifecycle, impacts, applicable laws and risk management from the certification body itself.
resources.use: Use the curriculum to identify knowledge gaps before selecting training; pair with actual risk-assessment and review work.

resources.title: 21 fairness definitions and their politics
resources.audience: Intermediate; governance reviewers and technical partners
resources.why: Explains why a single fairness score cannot settle a decision involving competing values and trade-offs.
resources.use: Watch before approving a fairness metric; document whose interests the metric captures and what it misses.

resources.title: Why AI Evals Are the Hottest New Skill for Product Builders
resources.access: Free YouTube video; newsletter page/transcript marked paid
resources.audience: Beginner–intermediate; governance reviewers, product owners and assurance teams
resources.why: An accessible demonstration of reviewing real traces, discovering failures and turning evaluation criteria into explicit requirements.
resources.use: Start at 16:51 for error analysis; ask what evidence would justify accepting or rejecting an AI release.

resources.title: AI procurement with Dr. Cari Miller
resources.access: Free; platform accounts may be needed for some listening features
resources.audience: Beginner–intermediate; procurement, third-party risk and governance teams
resources.why: Connects AI governance to vendor due diligence, unmanaged entry points and the evidence needed to challenge supplier claims.
resources.use: Turn the discussion into vendor questions about intended use, testing, documentation and ownership.

resources.title: A Deep Dive Into IVOs with Fathom's Bri Treece
resources.audience: Intermediate; assurance, policy and governance professionals
resources.why: Examines independent verification as a mechanism for checking AI developers' claims and discusses relevant regulatory analogies.
resources.use: Start at 5:32 for the proposed Independent Verification Organization model; assess reviewer independence, evidence access and accountability.

resources.title: Introduction to the NIST AI RMF 1.0: An Explainer Video
resources.audience: Beginners and anyone onboarding colleagues to AI governance
resources.why: A direct introduction from the framework's publisher makes a useful common starting point for a governance discussion.
resources.use: Watch before reading the framework, then name one decision your team must make under each of its four functions.

resources.title: AI Snake Oil
resources.publisher: Arvind Narayanan and Sayash Kapoor / Princeton University Press
resources.format: Book; free introductory chapter and companion exercises
resources.access: Paid book; free first chapter and selected companion material
resources.audience: Beginner–intermediate; all governance practitioners
resources.why: Builds disciplined skepticism about AI capability claims and distinguishes risks across predictive and generative applications.
resources.use: Read the introduction first; use its questions to challenge a vendor's validation evidence and suitability claims.

resources.title: The Alignment Problem: Machine Learning and Human Values
resources.access: Paid; may be available through public libraries
resources.audience: Beginner–intermediate; practitioners who need conceptual depth
resources.why: Makes specification failures, bias and mismatches between human intent and machine behavior understandable through research history and cases.
resources.use: Use it to sharpen questions about objectives, proxy measures and unintended consequences during design and deployment reviews.

resources.title: Fairness and Machine Learning: Limitations and Opportunities
resources.publisher: Solon Barocas, Moritz Hardt and Arvind Narayanan / MIT Press
resources.access: Free full online text and PDF (CC BY-NC-ND 4.0); paid print edition
resources.audience: Intermediate–advanced; governance and technical assurance teams
resources.why: Explains the limits of fairness metrics, the legitimacy of automated decisions, discrimination testing and data practices.
resources.use: Start with chapters 2, 7 and 9; use the discussion prompts when reviewing decisions that affect people's opportunities. Its legal discussion focuses on the United States.

resources.title: NIST Software and AI Agent Identity and Authorization
resources.format: Draft concept paper and ongoing research project
resources.audience: IAM, security architects, governance
resources.why: Frames agent identity and authorization as enterprise design problems that require applying and extending established identity practices.
resources.use: Use the proposed use cases to structure identity and access questions for agent suppliers and follow the developing guidance. The concept paper is exploratory work, not a final standard.

resources.title: AI Governance Dashboard
resources.access: Free newsletter; MyIAPP account to subscribe; linked content may require membership
resources.audience: All levels; governance, legal, privacy and risk professionals
resources.why: A focused stream of governance developments reduces reliance on generic AI news and helps identify policy changes worth investigating.
resources.use: Select AI Governance Dashboard; review relevant items against the original regulator or standards-body publication before updating controls.

resources.title: AI as Normal Technology
resources.audience: Intermediate; reviewers assessing evidence and public AI claims
resources.why: A useful counterweight to vendor marketing, with scrutiny of evaluation methods, predictive claims and the gap between demonstrations and deployment.
resources.use: Read the linked evidence and distinguish empirical criticism from the authors' broader forecasts.

resources.title: GovAI research library
resources.publisher: Centre for the Governance of AI
resources.access: Free public research; some linked publications may have separate access terms
resources.audience: Intermediate–advanced; governance researchers and policy specialists
resources.why: A concentrated source for governance infrastructure, third-party assurance, agent visibility and incident analysis.
resources.use: Start with 'Visibility into AI Agents' and 'Incident Analysis for AI Agents'; use the library to follow the evidence and open questions behind governance proposals.

resources.title: The 2026 AI Index Report
resources.audience: Governance leaders, educators and anyone preparing an evidence-based briefing
resources.why: Provides data and analysis on AI capabilities, responsible AI measurement and policy developments.
resources.use: Start with chapters 3 (Responsible AI) and 8 (Policy and Governance); trace any statistic to its dataset, observation year and methodology before citing it.
